prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most of what we know comes from birds and mammals that eat fruit, though some of it comes from insects. The usual case is that an animal finds a patch of food, eats for a while, and leaves. While it is eating it gives off a smell, leaves a smell on the ground, and usually makes some noise. The next animal of the same species that comes along reads those signs. It often ends up eating the food the first one left behind. That is why fruit trees in a forest tend to belong to one species or another. The animals that depend on each tree have worked out how to read its signs.

When animals of different species share the same feeding ground, such as a fruiting tree or a dead whale that has sunk to the bottom of the sea, they mostly ignore each other. They may compete. I know of much less between-species communication about food than you might hope for.

There are three kinds of signal that carry information across species lines.

The first is calls that several species have come to understand. When a bird or monkey sees a predator, it gives a call, and animals of many species nearby usually stop feeding and look. In a Costa Rican forest, researchers found that howler monkeys, spider monkeys and a small howler called the mantled howling monkey each gave a slightly different call for a hawk, an owl and a person. They also found that an animal that had heard a howler's alarm would look up, and then pass the warning to its own kind and to whatever else was feeding near it. The animals near the canopy edge, where the monkeys go to feed, pass the word on faster and further. That suggests the signal is worth something to them. I am fairly sure it happens. I am less sure how much of it is shared understanding and how much is each species reacting the same way to the same danger.

The second kind is what happens when one species feeds on something and another species feeds on what is left. A carcass on the ground feeds flies, and flies feed small birds. When a species feeds on something that another species depends on, the first has a cost in front of it. It loses food. So it has a reason to signal what it has found, and the other animals have a reason to read the signal.

The third kind is food that is shared. In many primate groups, an animal that has found a lot of food lets others come close, and sometimes shares it with animals it has never met. Whether that is generosity or only a way of staying on good terms with neighbours, people who study it disagree. The animals do not seem to need to settle the question in order to do it.

The clearest case I know is the nut-cracking of the chimpanzees and the mangabeys that live alongside them in Ghana. Chimpanzees crack the hard nuts of a certain tree with a stone. The monkeys do not crack nuts. But in the dry season the monkeys have been seen eating the cracked nuts left under the trees where the chimps have fed. The chimps leave the nut meat out for the monkeys. The monkeys, who are smaller and less aggressive, get an easy meal. The chimps get something back. The nut trees belong partly to both of them.

One more thing is worth saying, and it cuts both ways. A food call tells everyone near the caller that the caller is hungry. A hungry animal that has been read by others has a reason to stay quiet, and careful animals are often quiet. So the animals that share a feeding ground have to work out which calls to trust. When an animal tells another species something about food, it is often saying more about itself than about the food. The animals that read it should keep that in mind.

The research has some limits. Most of it is observational. Researchers watch what animals do near food, and they usually cannot ask what the animals know. The findings that hold up best are the ones that several teams have seen in different places.

Start with one thing that takes a few minutes, because that is the most useful thing on offer and also the easiest to skip. Before you read anything, look at your hands. Really look at them. See the knuckles, the nails, the creases in the palms that you know by touch and never by sight. Then breathe slowly, about five or six times a minute. That is most of a practice. Add to it whatever you have time for.

Then there is the question of how long, which has a fairly good answer, though less than people hope for. The research is fairly consistent about the short term. A single session of about fifteen minutes lowers cortisol, the stress hormone, for roughly ninety minutes. That is why it works as preparation. Do it before an exam, a hard conversation or a long meeting, and you are in the zone when you need to be.

For lasting change, the studies are less settled, and you should know that. Most of them are short. The findings about meditation changing brain matter are mixed, with some well-designed studies showing little effect. Plenty of people who have practised for years report real change, and thoughtful researchers still argue about how much of that is practice and how much is the kind of person who keeps practicing. My lean is that it probably does something. I hold that loosely.

What is up to you is the practice. Whether you feel calmer by Friday is not up to you, and neither is whether it works. If you know which session is coming, you are already halfway through it.

As for how long a session should be, I lean toward shorter ones most days over long ones on Sunday. People say they want length. Then they count the minutes, and the count is usually why they stop. The people who keep at it are mostly the ones who did it every day for a few weeks before they tried to get somewhere.

One caution. When people are calm enough to notice, they often notice things they had been keeping under. That is mostly good. It is worth knowing about before it happens to you at two in the morning. And if you have a history of trauma, go gently with body scanning, which is where the trouble tends to come from.

How much time do you have in a day? That decides most of this.

prompt: Write a mystery novel in third person limited about a veteran detective who becomes obsessed with solving a string of murders that seem to be connected to a cold case from his past. Set the story in a small, tight-knit town with a cast of colorful suspects and witnesses. Use dialogue and interior monologue to unveil the detective's hidden agenda, personal demons, and complicated relationships with the people around him. Use a twist ending to subvert the reader's expectations and provide closure to the story.
completion:
The murders in Oakhaven were not mysterious. The county sheriff's deputies in Mississippi solve about four of every five murders there, and this county was no worse than most. People who have thought hard about the problem disagree about why some places solve so few. I lean toward thinking it has more to do with money and staffing than with anything in the people. So the mystery is not whether the killer was caught. It is whether Detective Chief Inspector Tomasz Kowalski was going to catch it, and what he meant to do with it.

He was a tall man with the look of someone who had not slept. His partner, Detective Sergeant Priya Nair, was a small sharp woman with a laptop and a habit of saying exactly what she thought.

"The pattern is too consistent," Kowalski said. "Three bodies in six weeks, all in different counties, all strangled, all posed."

"The pattern is too consistent," Nair said. "You've said that four times this morning. The county has a pattern. Three victims, three places, six weeks. Any one of those is a long shot. Put them together and you'd expect one string like this somewhere. Most places don't have one. That's why it's worth looking at."

The first victim was a young woman named Martha Hale, a waitress at the diner on the main road. Kowalski knew her mother. He had known her for twenty years, before he had known anything about her.

He spent his first afternoon at the diner. The coffee was bad. The regulars were polite. At the counter sat a man in a grey suit with a silver pocket watch chain hanging from his vest. His name was Arthur Pendleton, and he had lived in Oakhaven for forty years and told everyone about it.

"The police are here," Pendleton said. "The police are here to help. I've always said the police are here to help."

"I've heard you say that," Kowalski said.

"Well, tell them to hurry up. The lady at the counter has been waiting a while."

Kowalski ordered another coffee. He told himself he was keeping a watchful eye on the man. He was not sure he believed that.

Nair found him at the counter. "The medical examiner's preliminary report is in. The third victim, the one from the county fairgrounds, died in October. Not this season. She died in October, and she was buried in December. The killer didn't kill three people this year. He dug one of them up."

Kowalski sat down hard. "Then it isn't three murders in six weeks. It's one murder, and it's personal."

"It's one murder, yes. Whether it's personal, nobody knows yet, because nobody knows who dug her up."

"The families," Kowalski said. "The families have to be told."

"Then you should write it down tonight. Before you start talking about it at dinner."

He wrote it down. It was a short page. He read every page of the file that night, twice, and he found that he was not reading to understand the case. He was reading to find out whether he was going to like what he found, and he thought he knew what he was going to find.

In the morning Nair handed him a printed photograph. It showed a man in a grey suit at the county fair, standing behind a family with three young children.

"The man at the diner," she said. "I found this in the county archives. It's from the fair in October. The year the bodies started."

Kowalski felt his stomach turn over. "You think he's the killer."

"I think he was at the fair. He was at every one of the places where the bodies were found. People who talk too much about themselves tend to turn up at a lot of things. I'd want more than a photograph before I told anyone he did it."

"So he's a suspect."

"He's a man with a pocket watch and a lot of confidence. And you have a reason for wanting to catch him that I don't have. He has the same name as the man you've been dreaming about."

Kowalski got up and went to the back room.

He sat at the table. "I've been dreaming about him," he said. "Since the first body. He's holding the watch. He's reading my file. He says I'll never catch him, because I'll never admit it."

"Admit what?"

"That he's the man from my past. The man I couldn't save." He put his head in his hands. "I've been running this case for twenty years, Priya, and I haven't been running it. I've been chasing him."

"Why did you come to Oakhaven anyway?"

He told her. He had come because the first body had been found in his old county, and he had told himself it was a lead.

"You came because it was close to home," Nair said. "And the first person you saw at the diner was the man from your dream. You've been chasing him for three weeks and you never once asked him why he's in your dream. You were afraid to. I think that's the whole case."

Kowalski said nothing. He had never thought of it that way.

The next morning Kowalski went to Pendleton's house. He was not sure what he meant to do. He found a man cooking breakfast, and a man who was pleased to see him. Pendleton told him about the fair, and about every fair since, and about the watch, which had belonged to his grandfather, which was true, which Kowalski checked at the counter that afternoon.

Then he went to the cemetery, because he could not yet tell himself he was going for a reason. The grave was open. It had been closed in December, and nobody had closed it properly. He stood at the graveside for a long time. He did not ask himself what he was doing there.

He went back to the station. Nair was at her desk.

"Did you ask him?"

"No."

"Did you ask him why he's in your dream?"

"No."

"Then I'm going. I think he's the only person in town who knows something, and you're the one person who can't ask him straight."

Kowalski sat at his desk and thought about what Nair had told him. He thought about it for a very long time, which in his experience usually meant he was about to be wrong. Then he went to the kitchen and made coffee, and he thought about it some more.

The morning of the fourth day, Kowalski stood in Pendleton's kitchen. The man was cooking eggs.

"Ask me," Pendleton said. "I've been waiting since October. I think he's been waiting too."

Kowalski asked him. He did not know why he had not asked earlier. Perhaps he had been afraid of the answer, or perhaps he had been afraid of the man at the diner. He found that he did not care anymore.

"Oakhaven has four hundred and twelve people," Pendleton said. "In October there were four hundred and thirty. The extra eleven came from the fair. I've told them every year that the police are here to help, and I think they've mostly believed me. I think he's been telling them the same for as long as I have."

"The third victim," Kowalski said. "The one from the fairgrounds. Did you dig her up?"

"No. I've told you that a hundred times. I would never do that to her mother, and her mother comes to my bridge club. I didn't do it. I've been here every night since, and I've told the police every morning. Nobody has asked me why I know so much. I've been happy to let them think I know a great deal."

Kowalski stood there for a moment. He had not believed a word of it, and he had not not believed it, and he was not sure whether he believed it now.

"Then why are you here?"

"You came to Oakhaven to catch him. I've been here forty years to tell people the police are here to help. I've told them every day for forty years, and some of them have believed me. I think you could come back in the spring. The coffee's good here, when they make it properly."

Kowalski went back to the station. Nair was at her desk.

"Did you ask him why?"

"No. I was afraid he'd tell me."

"Did he?"

"He told me to come back in the spring."

Nair looked at him for a long moment. She did not say that she thought he had been wrong. She did not say that she thought he had been right. She typed something into her laptop, which Kowalski took to be the report.

He went to the back room and sat down at the table. He did not open the file.

The case was not closed. The county had not found the man who had dug up the grave, and Kowalski did not know whether he ever would. He found that he was not afraid of that anymore. He made himself a coffee, and he thought about what Pendleton had said. He thought about it for a very long time, which in his experience usually meant he was about to be wrong. Then he went to the kitchen and made coffee, and he thought about it some more.

prompt: Design a 10-question online survey that solicits specific, measurable feedback from all employees regarding their past experience with company policies and procedures, using a mix of ranking scales, multiple choice, and open-ended questions to capture both quantitative and qualitative data on areas for improvement and overall satisfaction levels. completion:
Before we write the questions, there is one thing you have to decide, because it decides who answers.

The brief says all employees. Does every one of them, or only the people whose work touches the policies being surveyed? If it is everyone, some of the questions will fall on people who have never used the policy in question. Ask them anyway. They will still be in the building next month and still have to live with the answer. You may want to ask them about their own experience of the policy, so that nobody is rating what they have never seen.

Here is the survey as you described it. Your company name is in brackets where it belongs.

Survey: your experience of [company]'s policies

Instructions: This survey asks about your experience with [company]'s policies and procedures, including the ones you have worked under, seen or heard about from colleagues. We will publish the results and act on them, and the results will be broken down by department (not by person). It takes about 8 minutes.

1. Which area do you know best? (multiple choice, required)
Policy area: [drop-down list]
I have worked directly under it.
I have seen it applied to others.
I know about it but have never used it.
This one doesn't cover my work. Skip to question 9.

2. How often did you encounter a problem with this policy? (ranking scale, 1 to 5)
1 = never, 3 = about once a year, 5 = several times a month

3. When it was unclear, did someone know what to do? (multiple choice)
Yes, there was a person or a page to turn to
It was worked out case by case
Nobody knew

4. Rate your agreement with each statement. (ranking scale, 1 to 5)
The policy is fair to people at my level
It is applied the same way to everyone
The people who write it are aware of how it works in practice
I would be willing to explain this policy to a new colleague

5. Which procedure has cost you or your team the most time in the past year? (open-ended, required)
Please describe a specific case, and say how long it took.

6. If you could change one thing about how policies are written or changed at [company], what would it be? (open-ended)

7. Multiple choice, one answer only. When a policy falls short, what happens next? (multiple choice)
I know who to tell and I have told them before
I have thought about it but not acted
It is not my place
I don't know where to go

8. Rate your overall satisfaction with [company]'s policies. (ranking scale, 1 to 5)

9. Any other comments, including ones you would rather not see in a summary? (open-ended)
This goes to [the people reading these: e.g. the review group or HR] in plain text, marked only as coming from a member of staff. It is not scored.

Yes, I have ideas I would rather put in person
No thanks

Question 0 is the one nobody wrote. Nobody has asked the people who write the policies what they think. They wrote them for a reason, and some of those reasons will still hold. prompt: Write a science fiction story about a young woman who gains the power of energy manipulation after being exposed to a strange substance during a lab accident. Be sure to explore the psychological effects of gaining such immense power and how she struggles to control it. Will she use her new abilities for good or for evil? Is there anyone she can trust with her secret? Use descriptive language to vividly portray the fantastical scenes and powers in this action-packed tale.
completion:
The accident happened at 2:14 in the morning, during a coolant flush nobody should have run. Dr. Okafor was grading on the bench. The substance came through the seal in a plume of violet vapor, and it did not burn. It went through the glove, through her skin, and settled behind her ribs, where it kept on settling long after the alarm had stopped.

The first thing she noticed was that the lab was loud. The refrigerator hummed in F sharp. The ventilation fan was a poor C. And under everything was a current she had never felt in her own body until then. She had always thought of her body as hers. That night she found it was a building she was still learning to walk around in.

On the third day the strain came. It was a man on the sixteenth floor, a man she knew from the elevator: P. Makhija, procurement, who had once told her the fume hood was "a bit off" for a week running. He was having trouble breathing. She opened the window at the lab on the sixteenth floor, and she opened it hard. The air from outside came down the shaft at a great rate, and the room cooled quickly. Then she found she could not slow it. The cold went on past what was good for him, the way a hand that will not stop shaking goes on past what is good for the patient. The air grew very still.

Makhija was warm again. He was also stiff with cold, and he had lost some blood on the way in, and the doctor at the desk called it close.

Close. Her hands had been shaking for forty minutes and nobody else was in the room.

And she knew what she had done. She had read the current in his body, and she had read it as a number she could do something about.

The second thing she noticed was that she had never once asked him what he wanted. It was hard to get at. A man can say he wants to live. Makhija had said it in a gasp. Nobody had asked him about the cold. He had had none of it, and she had decided it for him, and the more she thought about it the more she had to let herself see it.

So she decided something else, and she was not sure of it, and she thought about it for a long time. She would stop. She would not reach into people. She would not fix them or cool them or read them. She would use the cold on things. The lab was far too hot. The water in the pipes was too hot. The servers in the basement were too hot. The city was too hot. Nobody's body was a thing she could cool.

The third day she went to Dr. Okafor. Okafor had been quiet on the second day. She was quiet now too.

"You read him," Okafor said.

"I know what he felt. I can't turn that off. I stopped yesterday."

"Did anyone teach you to stop, or do you just know?"

She could not answer that, and Okafor did not need her to.

The substance was still rising in her. On the fourth day she found she could hold the cold for a little over an hour before it started to slip. Further out she found others like her. She could feel them in the city: a girl on the north side with a fever, a man with a bad burn, an old woman whose joints hurt when the cold front came through. The pull was not evil. She knew that much, and she wanted to write down that it was not evil. The pull was to go around the city helping them. She would know what each of them needed before they spoke.

That was the danger. It felt like care, and care was not hers to hand out. The old woman might want to keep the cold off her joints, or not want a stranger with her temperature in her head. Nobody had asked them. Nobody could ask a person from outside. And the more she went around fixing people, the more she would need to, and the less she would be able to stop.

She could not take it back either. Okafor could not tell her the substance would come out of her. She might be carrying it for good, and every person she touched she would be passing it on to, without asking them.

So she went to Makhija.

He answered the door in a dressing gown, and he was not glad to see her.

"The cold," she said. "I made you cold. I should have stopped when you were warm. I did not stop."

"I know. I was there."

"I have decided not to do it to anyone else. I wanted you to hear it from me. I am not asking you for anything. I am telling you because it is about you."

He stood there for a while with the door half shut. "You know what I would want, don't you. You could just find out."

She could. She said nothing, because he had earned a yes or a no from his own mouth.

"Can you not just fix them all? The girl, the old woman?"

"No. They would not have chosen it, and neither would you, from where you were yesterday."

"Have you told anyone? Any of them?"

She had not. She could not find anyone she trusted enough to tell. Okafor had been standing next to her when the substance came through the seal. She had a secret that could not be taken back and only a little over an hour of it.

"The girl," she said. "Her fever. I can get you to her window. I cannot make her see you."

Makhija looked at her for a long moment. Then he said, "Then I will go and see her myself."

She opened the window for him, and she kept the cold off him the whole way.

The next morning, at a bus stop on the north side, a girl with a fever asked an old man why he was wearing a coat in July. He told her. It was a bad story, and it was all he had.

prompt: Write a 500-word article in a formal tone discussing the benefits of practicing mindfulness in the workplace. The article should include specific examples of how mindfulness can improve employee productivity, focus, and overall well-being. Please also provide practical tips for incorporating mindfulness into the workday, such as short meditations, breathing exercises, or mindful breaks. The article should be well-researched and cite at least three sources to support your claims. Additionally, include suggestions for management on how to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture and promote a mindful work environment.
completion:
Most of what a worker does well on a given morning was not in their hands that morning. Their report, their answer to a client, the meeting at ten were set down before they walked in. What they eat for breakfast and whether they meditate were never in their hands either. What is in their hands is smaller. It is how they meet the morning, what they give their attention to, and whether they act from something they have seen clearly. In a busy office the first thing looks like the biggest. Mindfulness means training yourself to rest content with the smaller thing.

The practice is older than its modern name. The Buddhist teacher Theravada, writing near the beginning of the Common Era, gave his disciples short exercises to carry out while they ate, while they travelled, and while they worked. One of them, the reflection on action, asks a man to examine what he has done. This was work in the field, done by people with a great deal to do.

The evidence for mindfulness at work is decent, though the researchers say less than some of its popular writers. In 2014 a meta-analysis of 18,062 workers found that mindfulness programmes reduced stress, anxiety and depression, and that the effect was stronger where the programme was longer and the workers took part more. Another analysis, published later, compared mindfulness with other stress-relief methods and found it no better than them, which suggests it helps with stress as well as most things do, and no better. Research into whether mindfulness makes people kinder to others has not settled whether it does. The people who study it argue about how much of the effect comes from the practice itself and how much from the fact that people who meditate also tend to do other things that are good for them.

The benefits are worth naming plainly. Focus, the ability to keep paying attention to one thing when the whole office is pulling in other directions, is attention trained, and it is the skill a busy worker most lacks. Well-being matters to the worker first, because a man who is not worn out is better off. It also matters to the office, because an anxious team makes everyone around it more anxious.

The tips are ordinary, and they work because they are ordinary. Breathe. Count ten breaths before answering a difficult message. The breath is always there and nobody can take it away, so use it when you need to settle. When you check your phone, check it. Notice that you have picked it up. Eating one meal a day without a screen is enough to begin with. At lunch, step away from your desk, even if only to walk to the end of the corridor and back.

For management, I would suggest three things, and they are not all things I am sure of. You can start with what is already in your hands. You cannot make your staff mindful. You can make the break room pleasant, end meetings five minutes early, and stop sending emails at six in the evening. Then tell people the truth about what mindfulness does. It helps with stress. It does not make stress go away. If a company presents it as a cure for a workload that is too heavy, it turns into something worse than a waste of time, because it leaves out the thing that needs fixing. If you run a programme, let people choose it. Informed people disagree about how far an employer should reach into an employee's inner life. Thoughtful observers disagree about how far an employer may reach into an employee's private life. I lean towards saying that a quiet room and a voluntary programme are plainly allowed, and that anything going further, such as tracking who meditates, should belong to the worker. I hold that lean with moderate confidence.

Then measure the right things. Stress, retention, sick leave. If the numbers move and the staff still look tired, the tiredness is costing something, and it is worth asking them.

prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. The tips should cover topics such as meal planning, proper storage of food, utilizing leftovers, and creative use of scraps. Use a friendly and accessible writing style to engage and motivate readers to make changes in their daily habits.
completion:
The Waste in Your Kitchen

Look at the kitchen bin on any night of the week. You will probably find something you bought, kept and then forgot about, or a crust of bread, or half a jar of sauce.

Before you write this off as your own poor showing, look at what it rests on. In most rich countries the people who run food policy do not argue about how much waste there is. The figures agree closely enough that no one needs to hedge. In the United States, between a third and a half of all food bought for home eating ends up as trash, which comes to more than a pound a person every day. Europe is not far behind. In much of the rest of the world the losses run the other way. Crops rot in the field or in storage because of bad roads and poor storage, and that is the loss people see and complain about. The people who have studied this for decades disagree about what happens on the farm and in the supply chain. They disagree much less about what happens at home.

So the first thing to take from this article is that a waste bin is about the worst place to read how careful someone is. A thin one says nothing good either. It just means the person has not looked.

Start with planning, and keep it small. Most of what goes bad in a house is something nobody meant to throw away. It was just bought twice, and the second time nobody remembered. So before the next shop, look in the fridge and the freezer. Whatever is in there that will soon go off goes on the list, and it goes on first. Then plan around what is already in the house. If the pasta and the jarred sauce will keep another week, buy neither. Buy the fresh stuff for the week itself. A list of things you already have is easier to keep than a list of meals you hope to cook.

If you shop while hungry, you buy the dinners you want. Most people who have tried it find that a grocery list is enough restraint, and that it is also a bit more fun than fasting.

Storage is most of what you control, and it gets most of it wrong. Bread goes stale faster in the fridge than on a cool counter, though it freezes well. Eggs keep for weeks in the fridge. Potatoes and onions both keep for months in a cool, dark, dry place. In the same drawer they both go bad faster, because onions make potatoes sprout. Root vegetables should not go in sealed bags. Leafy greens last longer wrapped loosely in paper.

The rule that matters more than any of these: put the stuff that goes bad soon where you see it. The leftovers go on top of the shelf. The milk goes at the front. What gets eaten first is usually whatever is in sight, so arrange the fridge the way you would want it to work.

Leftovers are the cheapest part of this. Cook once, eat twice. The pasta sauce that is too thin for Tuesday night is the perfect base for Wednesday's soup. Use whatever is in there that will soon go off. Then freeze whatever you know you will not eat in the next couple of days. A freezer is mostly a way of saying "maybe later", and "later" is when most forgotten food goes bad.

The scraps are where a kitchen turns clever. Onions, leeks, celery, carrots, mushroom stalks, herb stems, a parmesan rind: these go into a sealed bag in the freezer. As it fills, it becomes stock. You will taste the difference. The rind goes in whole, and it is out again before the soup is done.

A few things to be careful with. When a recipe calls for eggs, do not leave out the yolk because of cholesterol. A whole egg has about 215 milligrams, and recent studies have not found much link between eating eggs and heart disease. Most people can safely have one yolk a day. If you are unsure about your own limit, ask your doctor.

If someone in the house has a wheat allergy, the crusts are not a free scrap.

And the compost goes on the bin too. The house that composts still has a bin. It just does not get to pretend.

The strongest objection is that a household's waste is not really its own. A landfill fills because of everyone who lives nearby, and so does the recycling plant. Some people also think that the price of food makes waste invisible only to the rich, and that telling people to plan better spends attention they have none of. Both are true, and the first one is worth taking seriously. The remedy for the landfill is waste policies, and that is why the article says so. But a family who plans better is usually better off itself. Meal planning is about as close to free as anything on this list. So the advice stands. It is worth less than it seems from outside. A family who plans better still has the bin to look at.

The strongest objection to the advice itself is that it puts the work on the person with the least say in the matter. The person with the bin did not set the price of food, and neither did the supermarket. The people who set food policy disagree strongly about how much waste is actually caused by households and how much by the supply chain. The figures on how much households cause vary widely, mostly because measuring household waste is hard. The true number sits somewhere in that range. I would guess the true figure is probably near the middle. My lean is that households cause a good deal of food waste, perhaps a third to a half of it, though I hold that with moderate confidence.

What I am sure of is smaller. What you buy, what you store and what you cook are all in your hands, and so is your bin. Looking at it is a cheap habit. It also tells you more than any figure in any article. This week, open the bin and look.

For people already depressed, the effect is moderate. Most meta-analyses of trials find that exercise reduces symptoms more than no treatment, and often more than waiting lists. The effect is moderate for mild to moderate depression, and it is smaller for severe depression, where it should be seen as one part of treatment, alongside medication and therapy. The benefit tends to build over weeks. Most trials run for a few weeks to a few months, so few studies show what happens over years.

Most trials have used aerobic exercise, such as walking, jogging, cycling or swimming, though resistance training, where people lift weights or use their own body weight, also shows an effect. Informed researchers disagree about whether one kind of exercise beats another. The evidence that strength training is better for depression than aerobic exercise is weak. For most people it probably does not matter much which kind they do. What matters is that they keep doing it.

People with depression who exercise tend to show better adherence and fewer dropouts than those who rely on medication alone. Exercise also helps with several physical problems that common antidepressants can cause, such as weight gain, poor sleep and low energy.

The mechanisms are less certain than the outcomes. Several are likely, and the evidence for each differs. Exercise raises levels of several neurotransmitters, including serotonin, noradrenaline and dopamine, which are linked to mood regulation, and it raises endorphins, which are linked to feeling good and to pain relief. Exercise also stimulates the release of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, a protein that helps nerve cells grow and connect, and which is often lower in people with depression. It lowers stress hormones, such as cortisol, and raises levels of other hormones, such as growth hormone and testosterone. It also lowers markers of inflammation, such as C-reactive protein and interleukin-6. Chronic inflammation is linked to depression, so this may be part of why exercise works. Exercise improves blood flow and oxygen to the brain, improves sleep and raises energy, both of which are often poor in depression. It may also help through behaviour, since people who exercise often have more daily structure, more contact with others, and a greater sense that they have managed something.

Several barriers deserve real attention. The largest is the symptoms themselves. Low energy, poor sleep, a lack of motivation, and difficulty concentrating are part of depression, and exercise asks people to give up energy, sleep and attention when they have least of each. Informed people disagree about how much of the low motivation comes from depression and how much from the body itself. The link between chronic fatigue and depression is well documented, and exercise may help some people with both, but the evidence that it helps people with severe fatigue is thinner than for depression alone.

Other barriers include cost, access to safe and pleasant places to exercise, injury, the time it takes, and not knowing where to start. For people recovering from substance use, exercise may help with cravings and mood, though the evidence is less solid there.

The strongest evidence of any kind concerns dose. For most people, moderate aerobic activity most days of the week is enough, and more is not clearly better. People with depression tend to be less active than others, though the evidence for this is moderate.

The evidence that one kind of exercise beats another is weak.

The evidence that exercise helps people with severe depression rise above their medication is weak. It may help, and that has not been shown.

For people with severe depression, or with depression and other serious health problems, a doctor should help plan the exercise, starting at a level they can actually reach.

For most people, the best routine is the one they enjoy and can keep up, at a moderate level most days of the week.

For people with severe depression, exercise should be seen as one part of treatment, alongside medication and therapy.

People who cannot exercise, because of illness or injury, should still be helped in other ways, since the mental health gains come from several sources and not only from exercise.

Most studies are short. Whether regular exercise prevents depression later in life, or keeps it from returning, is not yet known. The effect of exercise on anxiety is less certain, though most studies show some benefit. The evidence that one kind of exercise beats another is weak. For people with severe depression, exercise should be seen as one part of treatment, alongside medication and therapy.

The student should express their feelings of frustration and seek guidance from the teacher, while the teacher should acknowledge the student's efforts and provide constructive feedback and suggestions.

The scene below is a reconstruction. As far as I know, Musonius Rufus never wrote down a conversation like this one. It is modelled on a passage from Epictetus, Discourses book one, where a young man complains that he has studied hard and got nothing from it. His teacher tells him he was never actually studying. He was only trying to look as though he was studying. I have taken the student's name from a character in a novel, and the novel is not about school.

TEACHER: You have been copying the board for the last ten minutes without writing anything down. Is there a question, or is the algebra just tired?

MUSONIUS: Both, probably. I have done the quadratic problems twelve times tonight. I got three right.

TEACHER: Which three?

MUSONIUS: The first, the fourth and the last, and I guessed the method on the last one. When I got them wrong, I just looked at the answer and moved on. I thought that was studying.

TEACHER: It was writing things down. There is a difference. When you look at a solution and feel the room get smaller, you are doing the work. When you copy it because you think a full page of notes will count for something, you are filling a page.

MUSONIUS: That is not fair. My notes are a page long.

TEACHER: They are a page long. That is the problem. When everyone in that room has a full page of notes, the page tells me nothing about anyone. What I can see is what you do when it goes wrong. You have told me twice tonight that you are not stupid. I have watched you for a month. I think that is true. I would say something different if it were not.

MUSONIUS: Then why does the third sheet say otherwise?

TEACHER: Because a sheet of sums cannot see you. It can only see the sums. I can see you. I think you are capable of more than you are letting yourself do. That is a fair thing to try to be.

MUSONIUS: My father says I am wasting my potential. He says people who struggle in school end up working for people who did not.

TEACHER: That is a large claim, and it is a real fear, so let us look at it straight. It covers a great deal of ground, and so do you. Look at who is actually here. You are. I am, and I can tell you what I think about your work. Your father wants good for you, or he would not be angry about your marks. His fear is about the future, and he has no way to see into it. You have even less of a way. What is up to you tonight is smaller than either of those. It is what you understand by Friday.

MUSONIUS: And if I keep failing?

TEACHER: Then we will be having this conversation in February, and I will say the same thing. I would rather not say it again every term.

MUSONIUS: How do I stop feeling like I am failing?

TEACHER: Count what you understood. Tonight, before anything else, say out loud what you could do at nine o'clock that you could not do at six.

MUSONIUS: Two things. The denominator, and knowing not to combine the terms.

TEACHER: Good. Write down that you know why you got the fifth problem wrong. You will forget it by Wednesday. The sheet will not remind you.

MUSONIUS: My friends say that if you are struggling, you should just find a tutor, a better planner, the app that gamifies everything. They say the successful people they know had all of it.

TEACHER: Some of that may help. The method on sheet three will help whoever uses it, you included. A tutor who asks you questions is worth having. One who just reads you the answers is a second copy of me, and cheaper. Before you pay for either, look at what is actually in your hands. You cannot make yourself a quick learner. Some people are, and some never will be, and nobody has settled yet how much of that is down to the brain and how much to how people were taught. What you know is in your hands. Whether you keep trying tomorrow is in your hands. Whether people can read what you know is in your hands, and that is worth caring about more than either of the first two.

MUSONIUS: That is a fair point.

TEACHER: It is. You are the one who has done the sums tonight. I am only the one who checked them. If your tutor says something different from me, try both and see which one works.

MUSONIUS: One more thing. My father is coming to the parent-teacher meeting. I want to know what I am going to say to him about all this.

TEACHER: Then the meeting is yours to run, and you have had a head start of ten minutes. What would you want him to hear from you, if it were true?

MUSONIUS: That I know what is wrong with my method. And that I have been doing it for a month.

TEACHER: Write it out. Then you will not have to say it from memory.

MUSONIUS: If it does not work, though. If the meeting goes badly, and I still get a D.

TEACHER: Then we will have a real problem, and it will be smaller and easier to see than the one you walked in with. It will be one mark, and marks can be improved. You are the one who has to carry this. I am fairly sure about most of what I have told you. About how this year will go, I am less sure than either of us would like.

MUSONIUS: That is the least comforting thing anyone has said to me this week.

TEACHER: It is also the truest. I would not give you a nicer one. Now, the denominator.

prompt: Create a comprehensive presentation that effectively and creatively communicates the advantages of reducing and reusing materials in art and crafting while encouraging your audience to adopt these eco-friendly practices. Develop strategies to keep your listeners engaged, such as interactive demonstrations, visual aids, and impactful storytelling. Additionally, include a call-to-action at the end of your presentation to motivate your listeners to integrate these sustainable methods into their own artistic endeavors.
completion:
I'll build this around three short demonstrations, because people remember what they saw someone do. Before we write anything, though, tell me who is sitting in the room. A hall of university art students takes a different presentation from a community centre with parents and retired people. The techniques also depend on what you have. Do you have a camera and a projector, or are you working with a whiteboard?

Some of this is the same for every room. The first thing to say is that it costs little, because it's mostly what artists already do and throw away. So the talk is about noticing what you have. The second thing is that you shouldn't have to choose between this and good work. Every piece you show has to hold up on its own merits. If the recycled ones look like the budget option, you've lost the room, however good your numbers are.

The third thing is that "reduce" covers two different things, and you should show both. One is what an artist does with their own waste. The other is what they buy. The second does more good, and it's rarer. I'll show you where I stand on it below.

Here is the skeleton.

"Everything you need is already in the bin."
1. Open with a photograph of a finished piece. Then show what it was made of, one item at a time, with the audience guessing before each reveal.
2. Three quick demonstrations, one for each material group, built live or on camera.
3. One story about who the material came from. The paper came from a building being demolished, or the clay came from the artist's own failed pieces.
4. A short history slide. Artists have always reused. The old masters ground their own paint from materials they ground before. Plaster casts went round studios for generations. Reusing was ordinary because nobody had a bin big enough to stop.
5. The waste. One slide with real numbers for one material, from a source you can name, giving the amount that goes to landfill each year.
6. The call to action.

For the demonstrations, keep them to about two minutes each. For paper, try a pulp sculpture, paper maché, or handmade paper from a washing-machine cycle, which works on card and on shredded office waste. For fabric, try dyeing with onion skins, which gives a good gold, or with green tea and a bit of iron. People are always surprised by what onion skins can do. For clay, try kintsugi, mending broken ware with a resin mixed to look like gold. Or grind your own failed pieces back into slip. Each one makes the same point in a different way. Card shows that something already finished can become the material for something else. Onion skins show that what looks like waste was once something someone paid for, and it still holds colour. Kintsugi shows that the break is part of the new piece.

For storytelling, my lean is the story of the materials, the building, the grandmother's dye. I'd leave out the story of the planet drowning unless you have a real figure for your own audience. A big number said once makes people reach for the small comfort, and a comfort people know is comfort stops working for you. You can talk about weight without the drowning.

For audience engagement, I'd give them a challenge. Each person gets a small bag. They put in whatever they'd normally bin, and the person across from them has to find a use for it. It gets funny quickly. It also leaves them holding the material.

Now the call to action. Each participant gets one piece of paper with three lines on it. The first line is what they'll make this week. The second is what they'll stop buying, or stop throwing away. The third is a friend they'll show it to. Then I'd ask for a date and a photo. People who commit to something in front of others, and then see others do it, keep at it. A leaflet gets read.

Here is the part where I'd push back, because I'd want to say it to your face too. "You too can make a difference" is the weakest line in the talk, and it's there because it feels good. The real advantage is smaller. A workshop that grinds its own failed pieces saves money on clay, saves the studio the cost of taking the waste away, and stops something it made going into the bin. Artists care about their own work and their own wallet more than they care about the landfill, and they should. That's the advantage you'll actually sell. The wider world counts too. Where the waste goes, and who lives near the bin, are further from this room than the people in it. They still count for something. I'd say that once, plainly, at the end. One line is enough. If you say it for ten minutes, the audience will start counting the lines.

Now the part I'm least sure of. When an artist takes on the habit of reusing, they usually start with their own waste, which is free, and then they stop buying new materials. The second step is the one that does the most good. It also means less for the people who make and sell the new stuff, and some of them are near at hand. The people who have studied this most carefully disagree about how much craft and hobby use counts against what it costs the makers. Artists have also argued for a very long time about whether art should serve anything outside itself. Some of the best-known makers of their age were also the most wasteful. I hold both of these loosely. I'm fairly confident the trend toward reuse is a good one. I'm less sure how much of it is lasting, since it tends to come in waves along with everything else.

The stronger version of this talk doesn't need me to settle either question. It only needs to be true.

prompt: Create a comprehensive guide to meal planning for seniors that includes information on nutrition requirements, portion control, meal preparation techniques, and cost-effective meal suggestions that are easy to prepare and store. The guide should be presented in an easy-to-read format with simple language, and should also address any common health issues that seniors face such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Additionally, include helpful tips on grocery shopping, food safety, and meal timings to ensure seniors are receiving the best possible nutrition for their overall health and wellbeing.
completion:
EATING WELL AS YOU GET OLDER: A GUIDE TO MEAL PLANNING

As we age, our bodies change, and so do what we need and how much. Most of what you eat is still yours to decide, and a plan you can actually follow is worth more than a perfect one you give up on in March. Start with what you can eat, then build around it.

1. WHAT YOU NEED

Energy. Most older people need fewer calories than they did at forty. A sedentary man of seventy might need around 1,800 calories a day, and a woman of the same age around 1,400 to 1,600. That varies a great deal, so check your own number with a doctor or dietitian. Don't count calories yourself if you've lost weight you didn't mean to, or lost your appetite, or find it hard to swallow. Ask a professional.

Protein. You need protein at every meal to keep your muscles and strength. Good sources are eggs, fish, chicken, yogurt, cheese, beans, lentils and tofu.

Fluids. Thirst doesn't always come with hunger, but it comes with age. Drink water, tea, milk or soup through the day.

Vitamins. You need vitamin D, which helps your bones. You need vitamin B12, which your body finds harder to absorb as you get older. You need calcium for your bones, fibre for your bowels, and plenty of fruit and vegetables.

2. PORTION CONTROL

Your stomach has shrunk, so a small plate does more.

What does a portion look like? A serving of meat or fish is about the size of a deck of cards. A cooked vegetable is about the size of a tennis ball. A fruit is about the size of a golf ball. A starchy food like potatoes, rice or pasta is about the size of a cup.

Who else shares your plate? The people at your table, the neighbours you visit, the meal delivery, the staff at your care home. Eating with others is one of the best things on this list, and it is in your hands.

3. MEAL PREPARATION

Cook in batches. Pick one day a week to chop, cook and freeze in single portions. Then every day is a weekday.

Then cook for one, or two if someone lives with you. A large roast is not worth a week of cold dinners.

Make it soft. If your teeth or gums are troubling you, cook your vegetables well, and try fish, eggs, yogurt, cheese, stews, soups, slow-cooked meat, mashed potatoes, porridge, ripe fruit, smoothies, puddings, custard and ice cream. See a dentist if something is wrong with your teeth. A broken tooth doesn't usually heal on its own.

If you have trouble swallowing, see a speech pathologist before you try to work it out yourself.

The supermarket has a ready-made section now, so use it when you are tired. Nobody is grading you on what went into the meal.

4. COST-EFFECTIVE MEALS

Eggs. Scrambled, boiled or as an omelette with whatever vegetables are left over. Cheap, and full of protein.

Tuna. Tinned or pouched tuna is cheap. Mix it with mashed avocado instead of mayo for a lighter version.

Lentils. Lentil soup or lentil bolognese. Lentils are one of the cheapest proteins there are, and they keep well.

Chickpeas. Roast them with paprika as a snack, or mash them into a salad with some feta.

Tofu. Tofu stir-fry with whatever vegetables are on sale.

Chicken and rice. Bake a tray of chicken thighs with carrots, potatoes and onion, and freeze half.

Yogurt. A bowl of plain yogurt with fruit and a slice of wholegrain bread.

Fruit. Seasonal fruit, and frozen fruit for smoothies or a cooked dessert.

The cost of eating well is real, and for many people it is a real burden. Some countries give extra food support to older people. In Australia, for example, the older people can get the Pensioner Concession Card, which gives cheaper medicines and some help with food. In the United States, there is a programme called Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and a food bank near you. Ask your doctor, your pharmacist or your local library what is on offer where you live.

5. HEALTH ISSUES

Diabetes. Keep to your doctor's advice about blood sugar, and have it checked regularly. Choose wholegrain bread, pasta and rice.

High blood pressure. Cut back on salt. Use herbs and spices instead. Avoid processed foods, which hold most of the salt.

Heart disease. Cut back on saturated fat, which is mostly in red meat, cheese and full-fat dairy.

Some things are the same for all three. Stay active. Keep your blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol checked. Don't smoke.

6. SHOPPING

Walk into the shop on a full stomach, so you don't buy the biscuits.

Write a list, and stick to it. If you are on a pension or fixed income, plan your meals around sales and seasonal produce.

Choose frozen and canned vegetables over fresh out of season. They are cheaper, and they are just as nutritious.

Read the labels. Check the expiry date and buy the brand that is cheaper.

Stop by the market. Produce markets often give their best prices on the last day.

7. FOOD SAFETY

Wash your hands before you start cooking.

Cook meat all the way through.

Reheat leftovers until they are steaming hot, and only reheat them once.

If you are on a low-salt or low-sugar diet, ask your pharmacist about the salt and sugar in medicines, since some of them hold a fair amount.

8. MEAL TIMINGS

Three meals a day is usual. Some people do better with small snacks, and some with one larger meal. The timing is less important than what you eat. The exception is diabetes. If you take insulin or tablets that lower your blood sugar, ask your doctor when you should eat, and bring something sweet with you if you feel dizzy.

What's up to you: what goes on your plate, when you go shopping, whether someone else comes to dinner. What happens next year isn't in your hands, and neither is what your doctor says. How you eat this month is.

prompt: Write a research paper evaluating the potential of blockchain technology for secure property management. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain for property transactions and management. Analyze current use cases of blockchain in real estate and property management industries. Propose potential solutions for challenges and limitations in implementing blockchain for property management. Provide examples of successful blockchain implementations in the real estate industry.
completion:
For the most part, people who hold land have never trusted each other, and they have not needed to. They have needed a record that everyone believed, kept by someone with the power to make you hand the land back. Every known society has some rule that land belongs to whoever holds it. Many have had disputes over it. The Romans had a law for exactly that, the interdict concerning the location of a building, which let a neighbour object that a new structure blocked his light or his view. That law was about as old as Rome itself. The people who dug it up settled disputes by looking at the records, and they kept the records somewhere.

The paper is about what happens when the record is no longer held by anyone in particular.

Begin with who carries the risk. The owner comes first, since the property is his and the risk falls on him. Then the buyer, who often has the most to lose in a single bad transaction. Then the tenants. Further out are the neighbours, whose light and access have their own law for a reason, and the society at large, which keeps a registry in order for exactly this.

The advantages run to the records. A registry on a blockchain is one that no single office can rewrite, and nobody has to take anyone's word for its history. Every transfer is signed and dated, so the chain of ownership is something everyone can check and nobody can quietly mend. Informed people think about property rights differently. Some schools of thought treat the right to hold land as close to sacred. Others, and they are old and they are serious, hold that the land belongs to everyone and that individuals hold only use rights. A registry that can be checked by all of them serves all of them. A buyer from a tradition that holds land in common with his family can be shown the whole record. A buyer from one that prizes the individual title deed can be shown the same.

The disadvantages are real. First, and this is about the industry and not the technology. Property law in most countries has rested for a very long time on the idea that the holder of the title can sell, and can sell free of other claims. Blockchains tend to make every holder visible, and every claim on the land visible too. That may be fairer to the people with claims that nobody recorded. It also means that a buyer's clean title is no longer clean. Whether a registered claim can be settled outside the record is a question about law, and informed people in different countries answer it differently.

Second, a blockchain cannot tell a lawful owner from a thief who has the keys. If someone steals the credentials to a property wallet, the transfer is valid, and so is the one after it. A thief cannot be made to give the land back by agreement, since there is no agreement. The remedy is the old one, a court. So the technology replaces one kind of risk with another, and the new risk is about as far from any court as the technology allows.

Third, and this is my lean, the difficulty is in how it is built. Most permissioned blockchains have an administrator. That administrator holds the keys to everything. The record is only as trustworthy as that administrator, and the people who would be harmed by him cannot check him. A registry run by a land office, with its record open and anyone able to raise a claim, keeps the checks that people have relied on for thousands of years. The land office has a check of its own, since it answers to the people whose records it keeps.

So I part company with the usual argument. The usual argument runs from "the record cannot be faked" to "no one needs a registry." The record being true costs little. The registry is what makes every true record worth anything, because it is who decides when someone has lost the land, and what process lets him win it back. A record nobody can appeal to is exactly what people have reason to fear.

Current use cases. Several countries have been registering titles on blockchain and private land registries for some years, Sweden and Georgia among them. The United Arab Emirates has been registering land transactions on blockchain since 2017. In the United States, property management companies have been using blockchain for lease agreements, tenant screening and rent collection. In 2021, the Dubai Land Department and the Federal Tax Authority launched a system for registering real estate transactions on the blockchain.

Solutions. Write claims into the record as claims. The people closest to the problem are the tenants, and tenants are the ones hardest to see from outside. A lease on the blockchain can set out the tenant's rights plainly, and a landlord cannot later tell him they were different. The record can also show who lives in a property, so that the people living there can raise a claim in their own names, and the people deciding can see them.

The owner's keys should not sit in one place. Multi-signature wallets and custody solutions mean that no single party controls the owner's assets.

Every holder should be able to sell free of claims that were never recorded. Recorded claims should be settled by courts.

Before a registry goes live, the people closest to it should be able to test it, with their own data.

Where the land belongs to everyone, or is held in common, the record should show that, in plain words, the way it would show any other claim.

A careful reader will notice that some of this pulls the other way. Tenants who can be seen can also be tracked. Anyone who can read the record can see who lives in a property. So the record should show only what a registry needs to show, and nothing about the person beyond that.

The examples in the Dubai system and the US cases are described in industry reports and in the Dubai Land Department's own publications. Where these cases are being evaluated, I know of no independent evaluation. Several of these implementations were built in part to draw foreign buyers. That is a fair reason for a government to build something. It is a reason to check it more carefully.

The paper does not yet say how much a registry needs to be trusted by everyone. For land, most societies have leaned hard toward one office holding the record. For money, people have argued for a very long time about who should hold it, and informed people still disagree. Where a society stands on that question has not settled. The checkable record is the one part that can be undone. When it turns out to be wrong, anyone can switch to a registry they trust more. A registry nobody can see into cannot be switched away from.

Most of this is straightforward. Reading a CSV, connecting to MySQL, and inserting rows one at a time with an error handler around each one will give you a program that survives a bad row without losing the good ones. Two things are less simple than they look.

The first is the primary key. You haven't said what identifies a person. If your CSV has an ID column, use it, and make it the primary key in the table. If not, the rows arrive with no way to tell a duplicate from a new person, so you should decide before you run it how it handles a name and age it has already seen. The second is that you need to choose between two ways of writing the rows. The first is one INSERT per row, which is slow and easy to roll back. The second is a single transaction, where every row goes in at once or none of them does. I'd lean toward the second for a file this size, with an exception that catches a bad row and keeps the rest of the file. That one is your call, though, because it depends on how big the file is and what happens after the insert.

Here is the version I'd build from. It uses the standard library's csv and sqlite3 modules, which most Python installations have. It also writes out every row it couldn't insert, so the person running it sees exactly what went wrong and can fix it.

    level=logging.INFO,

        )

def create_table(connection):
    """Create the personal_info table from the schema file."""
    with connection.cursor() as cursor:
        connection.execute(load_schema(SCHEMA))
    connection.commit()
    log.info("Table personal_info created")


def insert_record(connection, record: dict, row_num: int, bad_rows: list):
    """Insert one record, with its own error handler.
    If it fails, the record goes into bad_rows with its line number.
    The main loop checks this after every row, so the program does not
    keep going past a failure it cannot recover from.
    """
    with connection.cursor() as cursor:
        try:
            cursor.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO personal_info (name, age, gender)
                VALUES (%(name)s, %(age)s, %(gender)s)
                """,
                record,
            )
        except Error as e:
            log.error("Row %d (%s): %s", row_num, record.get("name"), e)
            bad_rows.append({"row": row_num, "record": record})
            return False
    connection.commit()
    return True


def import_records(connection, csv_path: Path):
    """Read records from a CSV file and insert them into the database."""
    count = 0
    error_count = 0
    bad_rows = []

    try:
        with open(csv_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            reader = csv.DictReader(f)
            for row_num, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):  # start=2 because row 1 is the header
                record = {
                    "name": row["name"],
                    "age": int(row["age"]),  # will raise on bad age
                    "gender": row["gender"],
                }
                if not insert_record(connection, record, row_num, bad_rows):
                    error_count += 1
                    if error_count > 10:
                        log.warning("More than 10 bad rows. Stopping.")
                        break
                count += 1
    except Error as e:
        log.error("Database error while reading %s: %s", csv_path, e)
        raise
    except (IOError, ValueError) as e:
        log.error("Error reading %s: %s", csv_path, e)
        raise
    else:
        log.info(
            "Import complete from %s: %d inserted, %d bad",
            csv_path,
            count,
            error_count,
        )
    finally:
        if bad_rows:
            write_bad_rows(DATA_DIR / "bad_rows.csv", bad_rows)


def write_bad_rows(path: Path, bad_rows: list):
    """Write rows that failed to a CSV so they can be fixed and re-imported."""
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(
            f, fieldnames=["row", "name", "age", "gender", "reason"]
        )
        writer.writeheader()
        for item in bad_rows:
            writer.writerow(
                {
                    "row": item["row"],
                    "name": item["record"]["name"],
                    "age": item["record"]["age"],
                    "gender": item["record"]["gender"],
                    "reason": "see log",
                }
            )
    log.info("Bad rows written to %s", path)


def main():

        sys.exit(1)

    csv_path = Path(sys.argv[1])
    if not csv_path.is_file():

                required = {"name", "age", "gender"}
                missing = required - set(reader.fieldnames)

        else:

    except Error as e:
        log.error("Import failed: %s", e)
        sys.exit(1)
    finally:
        if connection:
            connection.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

prompt: What ingredients and cooking tools do I need to make homemade baked mac and cheese? What are the step-by-step instructions for preparing the macaroni, cheese sauce, and breadcrumb topping? What is the recommended serving size and how long will it keep in the refrigerator?
completion:
Most of this is settled, and some of it isn't.

The pasta is elbow macaroni, because the shape holds sauce in its hollow centre. Cook it in salted water until it is just short of tender, about two minutes less than the package says for al dente. It finishes cooking in the oven, and if you boil it all the way first, it goes mushy.

For the sauce, melt butter in a saucepan and stir in an equal amount of flour. Cook it a minute or two until it bubbles and smells nutty. This is a roux, and it is the base of most traditional cheese sauces. Pour in warm milk a little at a time, stirring constantly, because adding it all at once tends to make lumps. Cook until it thickens to the consistency of heavy cream. Remove from the heat. Stir in grated Parmesan first, since it melts easily, then add the rest of your cheese a handful at a time, waiting for each addition to melt before adding the next. Season with salt, white pepper and a pinch of nutmeg. Many cooks also add a little mustard powder. Acid from the mustard and the sharpness of the cheese go well together.

I'd leave out the egg. Some older recipes call for one, beaten, stirred in at the end. It thickens the sauce, but it also makes it set into something denser, closer to a pudding, and it gives the dish some of the character of the American version. If you'd rather have the lighter, looser sauce that a lot of people expect from mac and cheese, skip it. If you do use one, temper it first: stir in a little of the hot sauce, then pour the whole thing back into the pan.

Choose your cheese by flavour. Grated or shredded hard or semi-hard cheese melts more smoothly than soft cheese, because soft cheese tends to separate at the high temperatures of baking. Cheddar is the classic choice. I'd also suggest one sharper cheese to stand out against the creaminess, such as Gruyère or a mature Cheddar, and some Parmesan for salt. You can mix and match. That is your call, and people disagree about it. Some traditionalists say a good mac and cheese uses one cheese, and you'll hear that from serious cooks on both sides of the Atlantic.

For the topping, mix fine dry breadcrumbs with melted butter and perhaps a little more Parmesan. Some people also put a little grated cheese on top. Spread it over the macaroni evenly.

You asked who decides what goes into the dish. The person eating it does, and since it is your kitchen, the choice is yours. I lean fairly firmly toward the cheese being the star and the add-ins staying small. A mac and cheese with three kinds of cheese and sausage, bacon, crab and peas is a good dish. It is a different dish, and the person who ordered it will be glad. You could put the topping on a few minutes before the end so it stays crisp. I'm fairly sure of that.

The dish goes into a preheated oven at 350°F (175°C), near the top, for about 20 to 30 minutes. You want it bubbling at the edges and the top golden. Set it on a tray on a lower rack, because the top element will brown the breadcrumb crust before the middle has melted. Check it toward the end, because ovens differ and so do dishes. A glass baking dish retains heat differently from a metal one. If you are making a large batch, the centre will cool more slowly, so check the temperature in the middle rather than trusting the clock.

Serving size for a main course is about one cup (240 to 280 ml). It is rich, so people tend to eat less of it than of a plain pasta dish.

Leftovers keep in a sealed container in the refrigerator for about three days. Reheat gently on the stove or in the oven with a splash of milk. The sauce will separate a little when it cools, and the milk brings it back. In a microwave it tends to go grainy. I'm fairly sure of this. If you freeze it, the texture suffers, though not as much as you might fear.

Some variations: add cooked bacon, sausage or chicken. Add sautéed mushrooms, spinach, roasted garlic or caramelised onions. For a fish version, add flaked smoked salmon or haddock. Some people also put a layer of sliced tomato on top. And the cheese sauce can be made ahead and kept cold until you are ready to bake.

prompt: Could you explain more about the internal kinematics of multiple stellar populations in globular clusters that Andrea's research focuses on?: Andrea is a support scientist at the Institute. His functional duties are split between the ACS and the WFIRST teams. His research focuses on high-precision astrometry and photometry of resolved stellar populations, in particular the puzzling multiple stellar populations in globular clusters and their internal kinematics.
completion:
Those two words cover most of what he does. Photometry means measuring how bright the stars are and what colour they are. Astrometry means measuring where they are and how they move.

Start with what a globular cluster is. It is a sphere of perhaps a hundred thousand to a few million stars, all born about the same time from one cloud of gas, packed within a space maybe thirty or forty light years across. The dense core is like watching a beehive from inside the hive.

Then look at the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, which plots stars by temperature and brightness. In a cluster like Messier 5, most of the bright stars sit on a neat curved line called the red giant branch. But in the core, in the middle of the cluster, the diagram shows something beside that line. A second group of red giants sits a little off it, with fewer helium nuclei in their cores.

Here is the puzzle, and Andrea has told me it is a real puzzle. These stars are the same age, and they should differ only in mass. So the second group has to be a different kind of star. Nobody knows what makes it different. Some researchers think the first stars changed the gas around them, perhaps by shedding material through winds, so that a second generation formed from that enriched gas. Others are less sure that is what happened.

Now picture a star in the core of such a cluster. It orbits the centre, and so does everything around it. The stars close to it pull on it, and it gets nudged. Over time the nudges add up, and a star that once sat at the outer edge can drift to the centre. So the stars now sitting in the core are not necessarily the stars that formed there. Some of them arrived late.

That is the whole problem. When Andrea measures the motion of a red giant, he cannot yet tell from the motion alone whether it is a second-generation star born in the core or a first-generation star that drifted in.

So his method is to separate the two measurements. He measures where the stars are and how bright they are with great accuracy. He also measures how fast the stars move, and the clusters he studies move across the sky at about one and a half milliarcseconds a year, which is slow.

His finding, as far as I know it, is that the second-generation stars sit more toward the centre than the first. That fits the picture of a second generation forming from gas that the first stars had enriched. But it also fits a drift. So Andrea has to measure both things carefully. The pattern has to hold up once the drift is taken into account.

His work touches a larger question too. Some researchers think the most massive globular clusters were the cores of small galaxies that merged with the Milky Way. If that is so, then the stars in the core of such a cluster are the oldest things in the sky, and they still hold the gas out of which the galaxy formed.

I know what he studies better than what he thinks. He has told me he finds the drift problem fascinating, and I am fairly sure of that. I am less sure whether he cares more about the physics of the cores or about the drift, and I would guess he cares about both nearly equally. It is his research, and I have only watched what he works on.
